library(tidyverse) 
library(knitr)

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
# Support rendering from reports/ or from the project root.
project_root <- if (file.exists("data/raw/conflict.csv")) "." else ".."
conflict <- read.csv(file.path(project_root, "data/raw/conflict.csv"))
```

## Review of the files and earlier work

I reviewed `README.md`, `scripts/create_final_data.R`, and the existing reports. The README describes preparation of an analytical dataset for an armed-conflict paper, but does not provide a codebook, source citation, or data-release version. The earlier R script combines mortality, disasters, conflict exposure, and covariates into a country-year panel. The raw file `data/raw/conflict.csv` is the relevant dataset for counting distinct conflicts. The processed `final_data.csv` contains only a binary lagged exposure, so it cannot recover the number of conflicts in a year.

The raw conflict file has four fields: `conflict_id`, `iso`, `year`, and `best`. The earlier code treats `best` as deaths, sums it within country, year, and conflict ID, and defines exposure when at least one such conflict has 25 or more deaths. It then assigns that exposure to the next year. This is the definition implemented in the earlier work; the files do not establish the source's full substantive definition of armed conflict or which conflict types are included.

Each raw row is a record associated with a country and year, usually with a conflict ID and death estimate. Multiple records can share these fields. Without event identifiers or source documentation, I cannot confirm that each row represents a unique event, distinguish true duplicate events from separate events with the same death count, or explain records without conflict IDs. I therefore count **distinct recorded conflict IDs per year**, regardless of death threshold, as the main descriptive measure. This is neither a count of new conflict onsets nor necessarily the number meeting the earlier 25-death rule. A conflict appearing in several countries in the same year counts once.

## Missing values and repeated records

```{r}
#| label: data-quality
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
quality <- tibble(
  check = c("Total records", "Missing year", "Missing conflict ID",
            "Missing or blank ISO", "Missing death estimate",
            "Repeated rows across all four available fields",
            "Repeated year/conflict-ID pairs among identified records"),
  count = c(nrow(conflict), sum(is.na(conflict$year)),
            sum(is.na(conflict$conflict_id)),
            sum(is.na(conflict$iso) | trimws(conflict$iso) == ""),
            sum(is.na(conflict$best)), sum(duplicated(conflict)),
            sum(duplicated(conflict[!is.na(conflict$conflict_id),
                                    c("year", "conflict_id")])))
)
kable(quality, col.names = c("Check", "Number"))

identified <- conflict |>
  filter(!is.na(year), !is.na(conflict_id))
conflict_years <- identified |> distinct(year, conflict_id)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(conflict_years))
```

There are **`r format(nrow(conflict), big.mark = ',')` records**. Years and ISO codes are complete, but **`r sum(is.na(conflict$conflict_id))` records lack a conflict ID**. All of these also lack `best`; all identified records have a death estimate. Missing IDs cannot be assigned to distinct conflicts and are excluded from conflict counts, but retained when describing record coverage.

There are **`r format(sum(duplicated(conflict)), big.mark = ',')` repeated rows** when comparing the four available fields. These are not proven duplicate events: different events could have identical recorded fields. I do not delete them from the raw data or use their frequency as a count of conflicts. Taking unique year/ID pairs makes the main counts insensitive to repeated records and to multi-country appearances of the same ID.

## Annual counts and line graph

```{r}
#| label: annual-counts

library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
years <- tibble(year = seq(min(conflict$year), max(conflict$year)))
annual <- conflict_years |> count(year, name = "distinct_conflicts")
annual <- years |> left_join(annual, by = "year") |>
  mutate(distinct_conflicts = replace_na(distinct_conflicts, 0L),
         change = distinct_conflicts - lag(distinct_conflicts))
kable(annual, col.names = c("Year", "Distinct recorded conflicts", "Annual change"))
stopifnot(sum(annual$distinct_conflicts) == nrow(conflict_years))
```

```{r}
#| label: conflict-trend
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "Distinct recorded conflict IDs per calendar year, 1999–2018. Repeated records and appearances in multiple countries count once per year."
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
ggplot(annual, aes(year, distinct_conflicts)) +
  geom_line(color = "#236B8E", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(color = "#236B8E", size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1999, 2018, 2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = "Calendar year", y = "Distinct recorded conflict IDs") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

The recorded count rises from **`r annual$distinct_conflicts[1]` in 1999** to **`r tail(annual$distinct_conflicts, 1)` in 2018**. It fluctuates early in the series, reaches a minimum of **`r min(annual$distinct_conflicts)` in `r annual$year[which.min(annual$distinct_conflicts)]`**, and increases substantially after 2010. The maximum is **`r max(annual$distinct_conflicts)` in `r annual$year[which.max(annual$distinct_conflicts)]`**. These observations describe recorded identifiers, not a demonstrated change in the underlying incidence or severity of conflict.

The file ends in 2018. I do not append a zero for 2019: unavailable coverage is not evidence of no conflicts. The extra 1999 source year supports the earlier analytical panel's one-year lag for outcomes in 2000.

## Investigating unusual changes and coverage

```{r}
#| label: coverage-diagnostics
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
coverage <- conflict |> group_by(year) |>
  summarise(records = n(), missing_ids = sum(is.na(conflict_id)),
            missing_id_pct = 100 * mean(is.na(conflict_id)), .groups = "drop")
country_coverage <- identified |> group_by(year) |>
  summarise(countries_with_identified_records = n_distinct(iso), .groups = "drop")
coverage <- annual |>
  left_join(coverage, by = "year") |>
  left_join(country_coverage, by = "year")
kable(coverage, digits = 2,
      col.names = c("Year", "Conflicts", "Change", "Records", "Missing IDs",
                    "Missing ID (%)", "Countries with identified records"))

largest_changes <- annual |> filter(!is.na(change)) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(change)), year) |> slice_head(n = 4)
turnover <- map_dfr(largest_changes$year, function(y) {
  previous <- conflict_years$conflict_id[conflict_years$year == y - 1L]
  current <- conflict_years$conflict_id[conflict_years$year == y]
  tibble(year = y, added_since_previous_year = length(setdiff(current, previous)),
         absent_from_current_year = length(setdiff(previous, current)))
})
kable(largest_changes |> left_join(turnover, by = "year"),
      col.names = c("Year", "Conflicts", "Net change", "IDs added", "IDs absent"))
```

The largest absolute annual increase is **`r max(annual$change, na.rm = TRUE)` in `r annual$year[which.max(annual$change)]`**; the largest decrease is **`r min(annual$change, na.rm = TRUE)` in `r annual$year[which.min(annual$change)]`**. The turnover table shows whether net changes combine additions and disappearances. An ID added relative to the previous year could be a new conflict, a resumption, a coding change, or newly reported activity; an absent ID does not by itself establish that a conflict ended.

The jump in raw records from 7,682 in 2011 to 18,443 in 2012 is much larger proportionally than the rise from 173 to 203 distinct conflicts. Record volume then peaks in 2014 and declines, while distinct conflicts continue to rise through 2017. This shows why record counts would give a different trend. Countries with identified records fall from 52 in 2011 to 50 in 2012 and 45 in 2014, so the increase does not simply coincide with more represented countries. However, represented countries measure observed activity as well as possible reporting coverage; they are not a verified surveillance denominator.

Missing-ID records range from 125 to 143 per year. Their fairly stable count does not explain the later rise in identified conflicts, but it cannot rule out reporting changes. There is no source-version history, reporting-completeness flag, event description, or documentation of coding changes in this extract. Consequently, these diagnostics cannot separate actual conflict activity from changes in reporting, detection, or assignment of IDs.

## Sensitivity to the earlier exposure definition

```{r}
#| label: threshold-sensitivity
# Match the earlier script: threshold each country/year/conflict total.
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
qualifying <- identified |>
  group_by(iso, year, conflict_id) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(best), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(deaths >= 25) |>
  distinct(year, conflict_id) |>
  count(year, name = "conflicts_meeting_prior_rule")
sensitivity <- annual |> select(year, distinct_conflicts) |>
  left_join(qualifying, by = "year") |>
  mutate(conflicts_meeting_prior_rule = replace_na(conflicts_meeting_prior_rule, 0L))
kable(sensitivity, col.names = c("Year", "All recorded IDs",
                                "IDs meeting prior country-specific 25-death rule"))
```

The second count includes an ID only if it meets the earlier threshold in at least one country that year. It is a sensitivity description, not a replacement for the main distinct-ID count. Its death sums assume the repeated records are legitimate contributions, as the earlier script does. Without event-level keys, I cannot verify that assumption or safely remove repeated rows before summing.

## Observations and next steps

Distinct recorded conflicts generally increase after 2010, although record volume and geographic representation follow different patterns. The main count avoids inflation from repeated records, but depends on IDs being stable across countries and over time. The available files cannot confirm that stability.

Before interpreting the trend as changing conflict activity, I would obtain the original codebook and release information, confirm row meaning and the scope of conflict types, and examine documentation of reporting changes around 2012, 2014, and 2017. I would also investigate IDs entering or leaving those years using conflict descriptions and event identifiers. Those fields are absent here, so causal explanations for the jumps remain unresolved. No raw or processed data were changed during this EDA.
